explanations.explanation: Mockers it is, friend. The psalm says the blessed man does not "sit in the seat of mockers." Walking, setting foot, sitting: that's three steps, and he skips all of them. I think that's a man who knows exactly where he's headed.
Not elders, friend. Psalm 1:1 says he won't sit "in the seat of mockers." Elders never show up in this verse at all. The only seats here belong to the people who mock.

Kings don't get a seat in this verse, friend. The psalm says the blessed man does not sit "in the seat of mockers." Walking, setting foot, sitting, and the last one is the mockers' seat. No crowns anywhere in it.

That's it, baker. "His delight is in the Law of the LORD." Notice it's not a chore for him. It's his delight, and he keeps thinking on it day and night. That's a man who actually likes what he's reading.
Good guess, since a tree and fruit come up later. But verse 2 says "his delight is in the Law of the LORD." Fields and harvests aren't in that line. His delight is in what the LORD has said.

Nice try, friend, but the psalm doesn't say a word about neighbors clapping for him. Verse 2 says "his delight is in the Law of the LORD." That's where his joy comes from. I bet he'd say that beats a standing ovation.

Right on, baker. The tree is "planted by streams of water." Planted means somebody put it there on purpose, right next to the water. I think that tree never has to wonder where its next drink is coming from.
A mountain makes for a nice picture, friend, but it's not in this psalm. Verse 3 says the tree is "planted by streams of water." The water is the whole point of where it stands.
Whoa, friend, a tree out in the desert? That's a tough spot. But Psalm 1:3 puts this tree "by streams of water." Water right at its roots, and no desert in sight.
Close, but flip it, friend. The psalm says the tree's "leaf does not wither." So the leaf stays green and keeps going. The withering is a different story, and the psalm saves it for the wicked.
False is right, baker. Psalm 1:3 says this tree's "leaf does not wither." It's a tree by the water, so the leaf stays alive. And I think that's one happy tree.
Prospers, baker! The psalm says he "prospers in all he does." That's a tree planted by water and a man who's planted in the LORD's law, both doing well. Fruit, leaves and all.

I get the thought, friend, because life does get hard. But Psalm 1:3 says he "prospers in all he does." Struggles isn't the word the psalm picks for this man. It's a tree by the water, and that tree is doing well.
Rest sounds nice, I won't lie. But the verse says he "prospers in all he does." Like a tree yielding fruit, he's getting things done. Rest isn't the word here, friend.

explanations.answer: Chaff driven off by the wind
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! "Not so the wicked! For they are like chaff driven off by the wind." Chaff is the light, dry husk, so there's nothing in it to hold it down. The tree stays put by the water, and the chaff goes wherever the wind says.
A rock would be the opposite of what the psalm says, friend. Psalm 1:4 says the wicked are "like chaff driven off by the wind." Chaff doesn't hold still at all. One good gust and it's gone.

explanations.answer: A vine climbing up a wall
explanations.explanation: That's a creative one, but no vine in this psalm, friend. Verse 4 says the wicked are "like chaff driven off by the wind." The tree stays planted, and the chaff just blows away.

Flip that one, friend. Psalm 1:5 says "the wicked will not stand in the judgment." Not stand, so the opposite of what the card says. The "Therefore" in that verse points back to the chaff blowing away.
False is right, baker. The psalm says "the wicked will not stand in the judgment." It follows right after the picture of chaff in the wind. They're not going to stand, just like chaff doesn't.

True, baker! "The LORD guards the path of the righteous." Think about that for a second. The man isn't walking that path alone, because the LORD is guarding it. That's good news for anybody on that road.
Not false, friend. Psalm 1:6 says "the LORD guards the path of the righteous." That's a promise you can lean on. The path has a guard, and it's the LORD.
It will perish, baker. "But the way of the wicked will perish." The psalm starts with a man who is blessed, and it ends on a road that comes to an end. Two roads, two very different finishes.
Nope, friend. Nothing in Psalm 1:6 says the wicked's road gets straightened out. It says "the way of the wicked will perish." Compare that with the other road, which the LORD guards.
I see why you'd think it, but it's the other way around, friend. Psalm 1:6 says "the way of the wicked will perish." The road doesn't last. The psalm closes with that line.
